n: In this lesson we will study the basics of GC-MS. To introduce the topic, let us recall the chromatographic methods: TLC, GLC, gel chromatography, HPLC, GC-MS and HPLC-MS. GC-MS is gas chromatography-mass spectrometry; HPLC-MS is high-performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Key terms: EI, m/z, TIC, scan, SIM, retention time and library search. The working order: isolation from the object, calibration with an internal standard, injection into the injector, measurement in Scan or SIM mode, peak and library search, then recording the result in the laboratory notebook and table.

GC-MS is gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. MS is one of the detectors of GC, differing from the others in that it performs qualitative and quantitative analysis together. The substance leaving the column is ionised, and the ions are separated in a vacuum by mass-to-charge ratio, that is, by m/z. In ordinary GC detectors, for example FID and the katharometer, quality is determined only by retention time, and there is no information about structure. In GC-MS, in addition to the retention time, every peak has a mass spectrum, which can be compared with a library.

The GC-MS path passes through these stages: injector, column in the thermostat, EI ion source, mass analyser, detector and, at the end, the chromatogram and spectrum. The GC part separates the substances: the injector, column and thermostat belong to this part. The MS part ionises, separates by m/z and measures the ion intensity. The final result is the mass chromatogram and the mass spectrum of each peak.

t: GC part: carrier gas and column
n: In the GC part, inert gases are used as the carrier gas: nitrogen, helium, argon. From the gas source it goes through the reducer to the injector, from there to the column and the thermostat. The column is U-shaped, spiral or ring-shaped, 2-20 m long, made of glass, copper, brass or steel. The separation of substances depends on the density of the column, the nature of the sorbent, the gas velocity and the constancy of temperature.

By design, GC detectors are of four kinds: katharometer, flame-ionisation, electron-capture and thermionic detectors. The katharometer detects the difference in thermal conductivity between the pure carrier gas and the mixture with the substance. The change in the detector is converted into an electrical impulse, and the curve on the recorder tape, that is, the chromatogram, gives the quality and quantity of the substance. The mass spectrometer is also one of the GC detectors; its difference from the others is that it gives quality and quantity together and separates ions by m/z.

Two checks are made before introducing the sample. The tightness of the injector septa is checked with soap solution: no bubble should form. The microsyringe is also checked: 0.5 µl of acetone is dropped onto filter paper; if there is no drop, it is recalibrated. After that, the sample is drawn with a syringe from the air-gas portion and quickly injected into the injector block.

The efficiency of separation of substances depends on their distribution coefficient. The distribution coefficient K equals C liquid divided by C gas. If K is large, the substance stays longer in the liquid phase and leaves the column later. If K is small, the substance is retained little in the liquid phase and leaves the column early. Substances with a low boiling point usually emerge early.

Retention time is the time from injection of the sample to the peak of the substance. Under the same conditions, retention time is regarded as a parameter determining the quality of the substance. Adjusted time is taken as the difference from the peak of an unretained substance. Relative retention is given in relation to a reference peak. In temperature programming, the linear retention index, that is, LRI, is calculated with the help of n-alkanes.

EI is the most widely used ionisation mode in GC-MS; it is standard in almost all instruments. The electron energy is usually 70 eV. The ion source usually operates at about 200 °C. The pressure in the ion source is determined mainly by the carrier gas and is below about 10⁻² Pa.

EI works as follows. The filament is heated and emits electrons. The electrons emitted ionise neutral molecules: an electron strikes a molecule, and as a result a molecular ion or fragments are formed. The ions formed are pushed out of the ion source by the positive voltage on the repeller electrode. Magnets in the source direct the electrons and increase the efficiency of ionisation.

Why exactly 70 eV? The main reason is that many library spectra were recorded at this energy, so the spectrum is reproducible. The ion signal is strongest around 70 eV. If the energy is lowered, fragmentation decreases and the signal falls considerably. At an energy below about 10 eV, no ions are formed.

If an electron is knocked out, the molecule may form a molecular ion, M⁺, without breaking apart; it gives the molecular mass. Electrons of 70 eV break the molecule apart: fragment ions are formed from the excess energy. Bonds usually break at a weak place, so the fragments give information about structure. For example, CH4⁺ and CH3⁺ are formed from CH4, while in a long-chain hydrocarbon there is little M⁺.

There are three types of mass analyser. In the magnetic sector, ions fly along an arc, and the radius of the orbit depends on mass. In the quadrupole, RF and DC voltages are applied to four rods; ions oscillate differently depending on mass. In the time-of-flight, that is, TOF, analyser, the flight time over a set distance depends on mass, and a light ion arrives first.

The only job that a magnetic-sector instrument can do and a quadrupole cannot is millimass, that is, exact-mass analysis; for example, the analysis of dioxins. A quadrupole GC-MS can do all other jobs. A quadrupole instrument is easy to use even without deep knowledge of MS; this is its greatest advantage. That is why the quadrupole is becoming widespread.

We compare the two modes. Full scan records all ions in the selected mass range and gives the TIC; a complete spectrum is obtained. It is convenient for an unknown substance and is used in qualitative analysis. SIM, however, measures only the specified ions at the specified retention time. Its sensitivity is high and the noise low. SIM is suitable for the quantitative analysis of known substances.

In SIM, quantifier and qualifier ions are selected; this reduces false positive results. First the spectrum and retention time of the known substance are obtained. The quantifier is usually the most abundant ion in the spectrum. The qualifiers are the 2nd and 3rd most abundant ions. The time window is set around the retention time of the substance. The cycle and the dwell time are optimised so that there are enough data points.

t: Full Scan and SIM in one method: setup example
n: In the MSWS method, Full Scan and SIM are used together in one run. Full Scan scans masses 50-500 in 5-30 minutes. SIM windows are given for individual compounds: for example, naphthalene 8.53 min, window plus or minus 0.50, measured for 50 ms. To avoid recording the solvent peak, the acquisition delay is set to 5 minutes. At point 1 the scan is 250 ms; at point 2, from 8.20 min, with a window of 0.5 min, Full Scan 250 ms plus SIM 50 ms, 300 ms in total.

t: Two modes in one method: advantage and disadvantage
n: The advantage of two modes in one method is that the analysis is done once, the total time is reduced and less sample is used. The disadvantage: scanning in two modes leads to a certain loss of sensitivity. In addition, two sets of data are produced, so processing is better suited to an experienced user. The cycle and dwell time are optimised so that there are enough data points.

The final result of GC-MS is the mass chromatogram; it shows ion intensity against time. The TIC is obtained by adding the intensities of all the mass-spectrum peaks in one scan. The mass spectrum shows relative ion intensity as a function of m/z. The retention time indicates when the substance emerged.

The library search is carried out as follows. The spectrum of an unknown peak is compared with the reference spectra in the library. The search gives a list of substances whose similarity is above the criterion set by the user. The decision, however, is taken by the specialist. Using the retention index as well makes identification easier and more reliable, that is, it is confirmed by the index.

Full Scan gives the TIC; by selecting a TIC peak, its mass spectrum can be viewed. The spectrum is compared with known compounds in the library, for example NIST, and the unknown substance is identified. MSWS can output unknown peaks into the report and automatically search them in the selected library. The analyst reviews the result and assesses the likelihood that the match is correct. Example: the peak at 20.81 min is Cashmeran.

There are four identification criteria. The first is retention time, compared with the standard under the same conditions. The second is the mass spectrum, similarity to the reference spectrum. The third is the retention index, which strengthens the library search. The fourth is the specialist, who takes the final decision. Isomers may have a similar spectrum but different retention times. Library data are usually obtained at 70 eV EI.

Now examples of the main m/z ions from the book. In the mass spectrum of fentanyl, peaks at m/z 245, 146, 42, 189, 44, 105, 29, 43 are formed. Ephedrine: m/z 58, 146, 56, 105, 77, 42, 106, 40. Phencyclidine: m/z 243, 214, 200, 186, 166, 158, 84, 77. The table also gives ketamine, LSD and psilocin, which we will look at in the following examples.

We compare ephedrine and ephedrone. Mass spectrum of ephedrine: m/z 58, 146, 56, 105, 77, 42, 106, 40. Mass spectrum of ephedrone: m/z 58, 77, 51, 56, 42, 105, 50, 43. In both, m/z 58 is the base ion. The order and set of the remaining ions differ, and we tell them apart by this difference.

Mass spectra of benzodiazepines. Chlordiazepoxide: m/z 282, 299, 284, 283, 241, 56, 301, 253. Diazepam: m/z 256, 283, 284, 285, 257, 255, 258, 286; it is given in the book with exactly these peaks. Nitrazepam: m/z 280, 253, 281, 206, 234, 252, 254, 264. Oxazepam: m/z 257, 77, 268, 239, 205, 267, 233, 259. Phenazepam: m/z 321, 349, 177, 75.

t: Mass spectrum examples: LSD, psilocin, ketamine
Objects to which GC-MS is applied
n: Objects to which GC-MS is applied. The quantity of morphine is determined by GC-MS or HPLC-MS; in the book the sensitivity is written as "10-11". Codeine and narcotine are also determined by GC-MS or HPLC-MS methods. Isomers of hexachlorane and synthetic pyrethroids are determined by GLC, HPLC or GC-MS. The groups of examples in the book: opiates, heroin, psychotropic substances, that is, phencyclidine, ketamine and LSD, and pesticides.

t: Examples of GC-MS use: table of methods
n: The table of methods. Heroin can be determined by GLC, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and immunobiological methods. Heroin or its metabolites, 6-monoacetylmorphine and morphine, are determined by GC-MS and HPLC-MS methods. Codeine and narcotine are determined by GC-MS or HPLC-MS. The quantity of psilocin and psilocybin is determined by UV spectrophotometry and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Isomers and metabolites of hexachlorane are determined by GLC, GC-MS and HPLC methods.

An example of isolation: urine. To 25 ml of urine, 3 g of NaCl is added, and the pH is brought to 8-9 with 0.1 M NaOH. It is extracted three times with an organic solvent, with 30, 20 and 20 ml. The extract is passed through a filter with Na2SO4. The solvent is distilled off on a rotary vacuum instrument until 0.5 ml remains. The dry residue is examined by TLC, HPLC or UV. This is an example for pyrethroids.

t: Choice of sample: urine and blood
n: In choosing the sample, urine is usually taken for screening analyses. In severe poisoning or in case of death, however, little of the toxic substance may be found in urine; that is why analysis of blood is important. For isolation, liquid-liquid and solid-phase extraction methods are used.

The sample, that is, blood or urine, is extracted with an organic solvent, for example n-hexane, in an alkaline medium. The organic layer is extracted into an acid solution and prepared for HPLC, or re-extracted into an organic solvent and prepared for GLC. Tricyclic antidepressants are analysed by GLC on capillary columns. They are derivatised with trifluoroacetic anhydride.

GC conditions for pyrethroids. Column: Chromaton N-AW-DMCS impregnated with 5 % SE-30, glass, 130 × 0.2 cm; carrier gas nitrogen 30 ml/min. The thermostat is programmed from 180 °C to 220 °C at a rate of 1 °C/min, then to 245 °C at 3 °C/min. Detector temperature 260 °C, injector temperature 250 °C.

Both FID and MS can determine quantity from peak intensity or area. Quality is determined by retention time and spectrum, and confirmation is obtained from the library and the index. For calibration, an accurate calibration table with selected internal standards is drawn up in the book. The peak height depends on the quantity of alcohol, as shown in the GC example.

t: Interpretation of the result and the forensic chemical conclusion
n: Qualitative analysis relies on retention parameters and comparison with a standard; it is carried out together with physical methods, the mass spectrum included. The interpretation path: the retention times are compared, the m/z of the mass spectrum is checked, and the likelihood of a library match is considered. The library result is given as a likelihood of match; the analyst reviews it. With a doubtful result, the check is repeated together with the teacher, that is, the specialist. In the conclusion of the report, the toxic substances detected and not detected are written by name; the expert's signature and the time are put.

Limitations of GC-MS. Substances are required to be volatile and thermally stable. Similar isomers, for example naphthalene and azulene, may not separate well; for this 2D-GC or a special column is needed. As a solution, the retention index and the spectrum are used together. Spectra differ slightly depending on the instrument, parameters and state of the sample; the conclusion is drawn by the specialist.

Safety and quality control. The tightness of the injector septa is checked with soap solution; if a bubble forms, the septum is replaced in the presence of the teacher. The microsyringe is checked with a drop of 0.5 µl of acetone; if there is no microdrop, it is recalibrated. In SIM, quantifier and qualifier ions reduce false positive results. For the solvent peak, an acquisition delay is set. The result, however, is reviewed by the analyst.

About instrument settings. The menus and settings of the Shimadzu GC-MS, that is, tuning, temperature and ions, are not given in this deck. Open technical pages give the general principles; the manual for a specific model is downloaded separately. Photographs of your own instrument and screenshots will be added to the appendix later.

Case: cocaethylene found in urine. Urine was brought to the forensic chemical examination as the biological object. An isolate was prepared from the urine and analysed by the GC-MS method. Cocaethylene was found in the analysis. Interpretation of the result is carried out together with the teacher.

To conclude. In GC-MS the GC separates, and the MS ionises, in EI mode at 70 eV, separates by m/z and measures ion intensity. Scan is used to identify an unknown, SIM for sensitive quantitative analysis of a known substance. Identification: retention time, mass spectrum and library are applied together; the decision is taken by the specialist. The working order: extraction, internal standard, injector, Scan or SIM, library and area, entering in the table.

Five questions for review. First: what are the sections of a chromatograph and what is the significance of the detector? Name the types of detectors. Second: what is the retention period of a substance in the column and by what parameters is the chromatogram characterised? Third: how do the Full Scan and SIM modes differ? Which is convenient for an unknown substance and which for a known one? Fourth: why are quantifier and qualifier ions selected and how are they selected? Fifth: why must the analyst review the result of a library search?
